justification: Sourcing is clean and the compiler-diagnostic differentiator is real, but the article has a genuine near-duplicate-content problem against two sibling articles in this same repo, which is exactly what an AdSense/policy pass checks for. Originality vs. external competition: I live-fetched the actual top-ranking Microsoft Learn generics page (learn.microsoft.com/.../fundamentals/types/generics), which is itself the #1-2 result for 'c# generics' and the obvious page to beat. It explains constraints, variance and boxing entirely in prose plus illustrative snippets that are never shown failing to compile. This article instead reproduces six distinct, real compiler diagnostics as runnable failures (CS1503, CS0452, CS0453, CS0310, CS0029, and CS1961 twice, for both the 'out' and 'in' violation) driven through the site's own run-code harness, which the Microsoft page and the typical tutorial-site competition (GeeksforGeeks/TutorialsTeacher-style pages, which explain variance and constraints descriptively without executing failing code) do not do. That is a genuine differentiator, not a cosmetic one, though I could not run fresh WebSearch queries against those specific competitor domains this session (budget was exhausted before I reached this article) — my originality judgment rests on the Microsoft Learn page directly fetched plus documented knowledge of how this genre of page is normally written. Source integrity: all 8 front-matter sources are cited inline in the body (verified by grepping each URL against the article text — none are orphaned), and I independently re-fetched three of the load-bearing quotes against the live pages. The Oracle Java type-erasure blockquote (three bullets: 'Replace all type parameters...', 'Insert type casts if necessary...', 'Generate bridge methods...') is verbatim-accurate, word for word, against the live Oracle page — this was the most scrutinized quote per instructions and it holds up exactly. The two Microsoft Learn quotes ('the compiler checks types at compile time, so you don't need runtime casts or risk InvalidCastException' and 'C# generics are similar to generics in Java or templates in C++, but with full runtime type information and no type erasure') both match the live fundamentals/types/generics page exactly, including the second one's specific claim that the article leans on for its whole reification section. The 'Generics in .NET' quote ('generic collection types generally perform better for storing and manipulating value types because there is no need to box the value types') also matches the live page verbatim. No fabricated or altered quotes found anywhere in this article. Filler/ad code/keyword stuffing: none found — the opening sentence delivers a concrete claim immediately, there is no restated-title intro, no boilerplate conclusion, and the toolchain disclosure ('On this machine (.NET 10.0.401, Windows 11, x64) the boxed sum consistently ran several times slower...') is correctly placed beside the first timed measurement rather than as a stamped opening sentence, per the binding editorial-brief rule. No ad code or ad placeholders present. The crosslink to interfaces-vs-abstract-classes.md's static-abstract section is factually accurate as a pointer (that section does define static abstract Zero and operator+ as 'contracts for statics, not instances,' which is what the sentence attributes to it) but, per instruction item 5, it does not complement so much as re-run the same demonstration: that section's exercise solution already builds `static T Total<T>(IEnumerable<T> values) where T : INumber<T> { T sum = T.Zero; foreach (var v in values) sum += v; return sum; }` over int[] and double[] arrays, and this article's own 'Generic math' section is `static T Sum<T>(IEnumerable<T> values) where T : INumber<T> { T total = T.Zero; foreach (var v in values) total += v; return total; }` over int[]/double[]/decimal[] — the same method shape, the same constraint, the same T.Zero-then-foreach-then-+= body, differing only in variable names and the addition of a decimal array. A reader who followed the prerequisite chain sees this pattern twice with no acknowledgment of the repeat. Separately and more seriously, the article's own opening act — ArrayList vs. List<int>, summing millions of ints, timing the boxed loop against the unboxed one to prove 'boxing is allocation and copying List<int> skips' — is the same benchmark, doing the same job, that the declared prerequisite (value-types-vs-reference-types.md, listed in front matter but never linked from the body) already ran in its 'What a million boxes cost' section (List<int> vs. List<object>, summing a million ints, timing plus GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() allocation-byte measurement — a more rigorous version of the same point, down to the prerequisite's own closing line: 'Avoiding this is a large part of what generics are for: List<int> has an int[] inside it, not an object[].'). generics.md's version is strictly less rigorous (no allocation-byte accounting, just wall-clock ms) and never once points a reader at the article that already made this exact case in more depth. That is the kind of repetitive, templated-across-siblings coverage the AdSense rubric explicitly flags, and it is why this article cannot sit at 8.5+ as written even though every individual sentence and citation checked out clean. `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/csharp-dotnet/generics.md` passes (PASS, blocks=20, executed=14).

issues.location: Opening section '## What `object` costs you', the `box-cost` benchmark (ArrayList vs. List<int>, summing 8,000,000 ints) — compared against `value-types-vs-reference-types.md`, '### What a million boxes cost' (List<int> vs. List<object>, summing 1,000,000 ints)
issues.problem: This is a near-duplicate of the declared prerequisite's own signature demonstration: same shape of program (two typed collections, one boxing and one not, filled and summed, Stopwatch-timed), the same conclusion in almost the same words ('Avoiding this is a large part of what generics are for' in the prerequisite vs. this article's 'it costs nothing at runtime because the CLR keeps the real type around' in its opening paragraph), and the generics.md version is strictly less rigorous — it measures wall-clock time only, where the prerequisite also measures allocated bytes via GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread(), which is the more convincing proof of the boxing-allocation claim. `value-types-vs-reference-types` is listed as a prerequisite in front matter but is never linked or even mentioned in the article body, so a reader who just finished that article gets the identical benchmark repeated with no acknowledgment.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either (a) replace the box-cost benchmark with something the prerequisite didn't already show — e.g. measure allocation count/bytes for a generic method with an interface constraint (the prerequisite's own 'generic constraint avoids boxing' demo is the natural next step, not the repeat of the collection-summing demo), or (b) keep a short version of the point but explicitly build on the prerequisite with an inline link ('as shown for List<object> in [Value types vs. reference types](/csharp-dotnet/value-types-vs-reference-types/#boxing-a-value-gets-an-object-of-its-own), the same gap shows up between ArrayList and List<int>...') so it reads as a callback, not an independent re-demonstration.

issues.location: '## Generic math: constraining `T` to `INumber<T>`', the `generic-math` code block (`static T Sum<T>(IEnumerable<T> values) where T : INumber<T>`) — compared against `interfaces-vs-abstract-classes.md`, '## Static abstract members: contracts for statics, not instances', exercise solution (`static T Total<T>(IEnumerable<T> values) where T : INumber<T>`), which this article links to inline
issues.problem: The two methods are the same shape: same signature pattern, same `T.Zero` initialization, same `foreach (var v in values) total/sum += v` body, same `return`, called with `int[]` and `double[]` arrays in both places (this article adds a `decimal[]` array on top). The linked section is framed by this article's own crosslink sentence as covering 'static abstract members... applied here to operators and factory-style members instead of ordinary methods,' implying it's the complementary foundation this article builds on, but the actual generic-math code presented here duplicates that section's own worked example rather than extending it with a new angle (e.g., a constraint that isn't `+`/`Zero`, such as comparison or `Min`/`Max` operators from `INumber<T>`, or a case where `INumber<T>` matters because a hand-rolled interface like `IAddable<TSelf>` could not reach `int`/`double` at all, which the linked article's own exercise already explains).
issues.fixLooksLike: Pick a generic-math demonstration that isn't the Sum-over-INumber<T> pattern already solved in interfaces-vs-abstract-classes.md's exercise — for example, a comparison-based operation (`IComparisonOperators<TSelf,TOther,bool>`), a `Min`/`Max` reduction, or a mixed-type generic-math scenario — so the two articles are visibly doing different work with the same feature rather than the same work.
